timeline.notes: Once the movement pattern is owned this becomes ordinary load progression, so ACSM's 2–10% load-increase rule applies directly.

timeline.from_level: 20 bodyweight squats to depth, ankle dorsiflexion allowing a flat-foot deep squat
timeline.human_label: 3–7 months to a clean full pistol; 5–11 months including a weighted pistol
timeline.notes: Ankle dorsiflexion and single-leg balance gate this tree far more often than quad strength. Athletes who cannot reach a flat-foot deep squat should expect the top of every band until that changes.

variance_drivers.note: Straight-arm and pulling skills scale roughly with bodyweight at a fixed height. Athletes above ~85 kg routinely sit at the top of every band; lighter athletes at the bottom. This is the single largest driver on lever and planche trees.

Rate of adaptation is logarithmic. An athlete with 3+ years of consistent resistance training moves through early steps in a fraction of the listed time but gains little advantage on the last two steps of any tree.
Connective tissue remodels more slowly with age. Athletes over ~40 should read the upper half of every band and extend tendon-conditioning steps rather than compressing them.
Longer arms and legs lengthen the lever at a fixed bodyweight. Taller athletes commonly need one extra intermediate shape (one-leg before straddle) that shorter athletes can skip.
Below roughly 2 quality sessions per week most athletes stall indefinitely on advanced steps. Gains from going beyond 4–5 sessions per week are small and injury risk rises (arampatzis-2024-loading).
Video review or a coach correcting shape is repeatedly reported to roughly halve time-to-skill on balance-dominant work versus unguided practice (kyleweiger-handstand).

prerequisite_standards.name: Bodyweight squat to depth
prerequisite_standards.rationale: Baseline pattern and depth on two legs.

prerequisite_standards.name: Ankle dorsiflexion
prerequisite_standards.target: knee past toes by ~10cm, heel down
prerequisite_standards.rationale: The most common hard gate on this tree — without it the athlete simply falls backwards.

prerequisite_standards.name: Single-leg balance
prerequisite_standards.rationale: Separates a balance problem from a strength problem.

plateau_signatures.signal: Falls backwards at the same depth every attempt regardless of leg strength; heel lifts
typical_causes: Compensating by rounding the back instead of sitting into the ankle
resolution: Elevate the heel slightly and lower the elevation over weeks
Keep the box progression going rather than forcing full depth

plateau_signatures.signal: One side progresses two or more steps ahead of the other
typical_causes: Old ankle or knee injury on the lagging side
Always starting sets with the strong side
resolution: Start every set on the weaker side and match its volume on the strong side, not the reverse
Investigate the lagging ankle's range specifically

regression_triggers.trigger: Layoff or markedly reduced training for less than 4 weeks (illness, travel, work crunch)
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: No step lost. Hold times commonly return 10–25% short for the first two sessions; eccentric control and shape quality degrade before maximal strength does.
regression_triggers.action: Resume one step below your unlock for two sessions, then retest. Do not re-earn the whole step — strength-trained athletes show only limited decline at this timescale.

regression_triggers.typical_dropback: Force production falls roughly 7–12%, which usually costs one step on hold-based progressions and one to two steps on the hardest dynamic ones. Recently acquired gains are retained far better than the loss in maximal force suggests.
regression_triggers.action: Restart two steps below your previous unlock and rebuild with full volume but reduced intensity. Expect to regain the lost steps in a fraction of the time they originally took.

regression_triggers.trigger: Planned deload, or four consecutive weeks with no measurable progress
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: None. Hold times often improve in the week after the deload.
regression_triggers.action: Cut volume roughly in half and keep intensity, for one week. Overcoming Gravity's rule is that four weeks without progress means the cycle is finished, not that you need to try harder.

regression_triggers.trigger: Tendon pain forcing modified or stopped training
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: Highly variable. Time lost is usually 6–12 weeks because the tissue must be reloaded from a low baseline, and the affected step is typically lost entirely.
regression_triggers.action: Drop to the last pain-free step, reintroduce isometric then slow eccentric loading, and rebuild across at least 8–12 weeks — the window in which tendon stiffness actually changes. Returning at the previous intensity is the most common cause of recurrence.

injury_risk_timeline.mechanism: High patellofemoral compression at deep flexion on one leg, often before the tendon has adapted to the load
prophylaxis: Progress via box height rather than by grinding partial reps
Build volume over 8–12 weeks in line with tendon adaptation timelines
Keep the knee tracking over the foot rather than collapsing inward
red_flags: Pain under or around the kneecap during the descent
Ache on stairs the following day

productive.notes: ACSM recommends 3–4 sessions per week for intermediates and 4–5 for advanced trainees. Tendon work shows no additional benefit beyond roughly 2.5–5 sessions per week, so extra frequency mostly buys injury risk.

too_much_signals: Hold times shorter in week 3 of a block than in week 1 despite equal or greater effort
Joint or tendon soreness that is still present at the start of the next session rather than easing during warm-up
Needing progressively longer warm-ups to reach the same working quality
Shape degrading within a set — reaching the time target only by bending arms or piking
Sleep or appetite disruption alongside stalled numbers

deload.protocol: One week at roughly half the usual hard sets, keeping intensity and shape quality intact.
deload.trigger: Planned every 4–8 weeks, or immediately after four consecutive weeks without measurable progress.
